chapter_title: Navigating the Junos OS CLI and Initial Configuration
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the heart of Junos OS configuration! The Command Line Interface (CLI) is your primary tool for interacting with Juniper devices, allowing you to monitor, configure, and troubleshoot your network. There are several ways to access the CLI. For initial setup, you'll typically use a console cable connected directly to the device's console port. Once the device has basic network connectivity, you can use remote access protocols like SSH (Secure Shell) for more convenient management. Establishing SSH access is a critical part of securing your device and will be covered shortly.

Once you're connected to the CLI, you'll find yourself in one of two primary modes: **operational mode** or **configuration mode**. Operational mode, indicated by a `>` prompt (e.g., `user@router>`), is where you execute commands to monitor the device's status, view routing tables, check interface statistics, and perform diagnostic tests. For instance, to see the Junos OS version, you'd type `show version`. To check the status of network interfaces, you might use `show interfaces terse`. Other common operational commands include `ping` for testing connectivity and `traceroute` for path analysis. These commands do not alter the device's configuration; they simply display information or perform immediate actions.

To make changes to the device's settings, you must enter **configuration mode**, which is indicated by a `#` prompt (e.g., `user@router#`). You enter configuration mode by typing `configure` from operational mode. Within configuration mode, you build up a set of proposed changes, known as the *candidate configuration*. These changes are not active on the device until you explicitly commit them. This two-step process (configure, then commit) is a cornerstone of Junos OS, providing a safety net by allowing you to review your changes before they impact the live network. To set a hostname, for example, you would navigate to the `[edit system]` hierarchy level and use `set host-name my-router`. After making your changes, you must type `commit` to apply them. If you decide not to apply the changes, you can type `exit` to leave configuration mode without committing, or `rollback` to discard uncommitted changes.

Let's walk through some essential initial configuration steps. Every new Juniper device needs a unique identity and secure access. First, setting the hostname helps identify the device on the network. From configuration mode, you'd use `set system host-name MyJunosRouter`. Equally important is securing the root user account. The root user has full administrative privileges, so setting a strong password is non-negotiable. You can do this with `set system root-authentication plain-text-password`, and the system will prompt you to enter and confirm your password. Remember to choose a complex password that combines uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols. Failing to set a strong root password or leaving it blank is a significant security vulnerability.

Another crucial initial step is configuring Network Time Protocol (NTP). NTP ensures your device's clock is synchronized with a reliable time source, which is vital for accurate logging, troubleshooting, and certificate validation. You can configure an NTP server using `set system ntp server <NTP_SERVER_IP_ADDRESS>`. Replace `<NTP_SERVER_IP_ADDRESS>` with a public NTP server or one on your internal network. Finally, for remote management, you'll want to enable SSH. This involves `set system services ssh` to enable the SSH daemon. For security, it's also good practice to create a non-root user for daily administration and configure SSH to only allow access for specific users or from specific source IP addresses. A common mistake is forgetting to `commit` changes after making them. Always remember: if you don't commit, your changes won't be applied! Another common pitfall is incorrect command syntax; Junos OS is quite particular, but its tab-completion and `?` help features are invaluable for exploring valid commands and options.

screens.title: Navigating the Junos OS CLI and Initial Configuration
screens.subtitle: Connect, inspect, and make safe changes using Junos modes and the commit workflow.

narration.text: Welcome. In this chapter you'll learn how to reach a Junos device, how to tell whether you are in monitoring mode or configuration mode, and how to perform the essential first changes every device needs. We'll cover safe access methods, the difference between operational commands that inspect the system and configuration mode where you build a candidate configuration, and why the commit command is the single most important step before changes take effect. You'll also see concrete commands to set a hostname, secure the root account, configure NTP for reliable timestamps, and enable SSH for remote management. Practical examples include a simple console connection, an SSH login after initial networking, and a short hands-on sequence that ends with a commit and verification. Finally, we'll emphasize common mistakes to avoid, such as forgetting to commit or leaving the root password blank. By the end you will be able to perform an initial setup and explain the purpose of candidate versus active configuration. Think about a recent device you managed — how would you apply these steps the first time you power it on?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Junos separates read-only operational actions from staged configuration changes. Always verify and commit deliberately to move candidate changes into the active configuration.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives focus your time on practical skills you need to manage Junos devices. First, you will be able to access the CLI using a direct console connection and, once networked, by SSH. That matters because your initial setup often happens before network services are available. Second, you will distinguish operational mode and configuration mode, run common show and diagnostic commands, and build a candidate configuration. Understanding the difference prevents accidental changes and helps you test before applying. Third, you will perform initial configuration tasks: set a clear hostname, create a strong root password, configure an NTP server, and enable SSH for remote management. These tasks establish identity, security, and accurate logging. Fourth, you will understand the commit command, the candidate versus active configuration model, and how rollback works so you can apply changes safely and recover quickly from mistakes. Each objective ties directly to a hands-on step so you can practice and prove competency in a lab or virtual device.

keyIdea.title: Objective summary
keyIdea.text: Access, mode awareness, initial setup tasks, and the commit workflow are the minimum skills for safely deploying a Junos device.

screens.title: How to access the Junos CLI
screens.subtitle: Console for first-touch, SSH for remote management

narration.text: Accessing the Junos CLI is the first, non-negotiable step in device setup. The most reliable method during initial power-on is the serial console cable connected to the device's console port. This gives you a direct local session even when the device has no IP configuration, so it is essential when a device is new or recovering from a fault. As soon as the device has a management IP and network reachability, you should enable SSH for encrypted remote access. SSH reduces the risk of credential capture compared with unencrypted alternatives. A concrete example: plug a USB-to-serial adapter or a console cable, open a terminal emulator at the device's default baud rate, and you will be presented with a prompt such as user@router>. After basic network setup and assigning an IP to a management interface, enable SSH with set system services ssh, commit, and then attempt an SSH login from your management workstation. A common misconception is that SSH eliminates the need for console access — it does not. Console remains essential for early setup and recovery scenarios. Key takeaway: always plan for both-console-first access and secured SSH for day-to-day administration. How would you reach a new device that has no network yet?

keyIdea.title: Access priorities
keyIdea.text: Use the console for initial access; enable SSH after network configuration for secure remote management.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › CLI Access
Process

Console then SSH

Follow these steps when starting a fresh device.

  1. 1. Connect console cable to the console port and open a terminal at the device's baud rate.
  2. 2. Use show version to confirm boot and model.
  3. 3. Configure a management interface IP and enable SSH: set system services ssh, commit.
  4. 4. From your workstation, test SSH connectivity and login using a non-root account when possible.
Common-mistake
Assuming SSH will work before the device has IP routing. Always verify IP reachability before relying on remote access.
Key Takeaway

Console for first-touch; enable and test SSH only after you have configured an IP on the management interface.

Terminal snapshot
# Example operational check
user@router> show version
Junos: 18.4R?X
# After basic IP config and enabling SSH
user@router> configure
[edit]
user@router# set system services ssh
user@router# commit
Example shows starting in operational mode, entering configure, setting SSH, and committing. This sequence transitions you from local setup to secure remote management.

screens.title: Operational mode vs Configuration mode
screens.subtitle: What each mode is for and how to use them safely

narration.text: Junos OS exposes two primary CLI modes that are intentionally separate: operational mode and configuration mode. Operational mode is the read-and-test environment. You use it to inspect device state with commands such as show version, show interfaces terse, ping, and traceroute. These commands do not change the configuration; they let you make informed decisions. Configuration mode is where you build changes. Enter it with the configure command and you will work on a candidate configuration that only becomes active after you run commit. A concrete example: you might run show interfaces terse to identify the management interface, then enter configure and set system host-name MyJNCIA-Router and set system services ssh before committing. A common misconception is that typing a set command immediately changes the running device — it does not. That safety model allows you to assemble multiple changes, review them, and commit them atomically. When you want to discard uncommitted edits, use exit to return to operational mode without committing, or use rollback to revert to a previous committed configuration. Close by asking yourself: when would you stage multiple changes together rather than commit each individually?

keyIdea.title: Mode distinction
keyIdea.text: Operational: inspect and test. Configuration: stage changes in a candidate configuration and commit to apply them.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Modes & Prompts
Definition

Operational mode (read-only)

Use show, ping, and traceroute to monitor and diagnose. These commands do not alter the device state.

• show version — confirm Junos release and hardware.
• show interfaces terse — check interface states and addresses.
• ping — verify reachability.
Definition

Configuration mode (candidate)

Enter configure to stage changes. Use set commands to create a candidate configuration and commit to apply everything atomically.

• set system host-name — stage a hostname change.
• exit — discard uncommitted changes and return to operational mode.
• rollback — revert to a prior committed configuration if needed.
Example
Run show interfaces terse, then configure and set the hostname before committing all changes together.
Misconception
Typing set commands immediately changes the running system — it only stages changes until commit.
Check your understanding
When would grouping multiple related changes into one commit be safer than committing each change separately?

screens.title: Candidate configuration, commit, and rollback
screens.subtitle: How changes move from candidate to active and how to recover

narration.text: The commit workflow is central to Junos safety. When you change settings in configure mode, you are manipulating a candidate configuration — a draft that lives separately from the active configuration that the router actually uses. This separation means you can make multiple edits, run a quick show | compare to review differences, and then commit once you are confident. A concrete example: you add a hostname, set NTP, and enable SSH, then use commit so all three become active together. If the changes introduce an error, you can use rollback to return to a previous committed state. Rollback is useful when a commit causes unintended service disruption. A typical misconception is that rollback and exit serve the same purpose; they do not. Exit without commit simply discards uncommitted edits and returns you to operational mode, while rollback reverts active configuration back to an earlier committed snapshot. For safe practice, review candidate changes with show | compare, and consider commit confirmed when you want the change to persist. What review step will you add before committing in a production environment?

keyIdea.title: Commit safety
keyIdea.text: Stage edits in candidate configuration, review differences, commit atomically, and use rollback to recover a prior committed state if necessary.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Commit Workflow
Process Flow

Stage → Review → Commit → Verify

Stage: Make set commands in configure mode to build the candidate configuration.
Review: Use show | compare to inspect differences between candidate and active configuration.
Commit: Apply all staged changes atomically with commit.
Recover: Use rollback to revert the active configuration to a previous committed snapshot if needed.
Pro tip

Run show | compare before any commit and consider commit confirmed when you want edits to persist across sessions.

Command examples
# Inspect differences
user@router# show | compare
# Apply staged edits
user@router# commit
# Revert to previous commit if needed
user@router# rollback 1
Use rollback with care; it restores a past committed configuration and changes the active state. For simple uncommitted edits you can also use exit to discard without impacting the active configuration.

screens.title: Set the hostname and verify
screens.subtitle: Give the device a unique identity and confirm the change

narration.text: Naming a device clearly is a small step with outsized operational value. A hostname helps you and automated systems identify the device in logs, configuration management systems, and monitoring dashboards. To set a hostname you enter configure and set system host-name followed by your chosen name, for example MyJNCIA-Router. After staging the change, commit to apply it. Once committed, verify the active value from operational mode using show system hostname or observe the prompt which reflects the hostname. A concrete walkthrough: start from operational mode, type configure, run set system host-name MyJNCIA-Router, then commit. If you forget commit, the prompt and operational show command will still reflect the previous hostname. A common mistake is including spaces or unsupported characters in a hostname; keep it alphanumeric and dash characters for predictable behavior. Key takeaway: choose a clear, unique hostname, stage and commit the change, and verify the active configuration before proceeding to further setup. Set the hostname and verify means set the hostname in configure mode, commit, then verify with show system hostname to ensure the change is active.. In practical terms, give the device a unique identity and confirm the change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hostname practice
keyIdea.text: Set the hostname in configure mode, commit, then verify with show system hostname to ensure the change is active.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hostname
Code walkthrough
# From operational mode
user@router> configure
[edit]
user@router# set system host-name MyJNCIA-Router
user@router# commit
# Exit to operational mode
user@router# exit
user@router> show system hostname
MyJNCIA-Router
Example shows setting and committing a hostname, then verifying the active configuration returned by show system hostname.
Practical guidance
  • Use short, unique names that map to location or role.
  • Avoid spaces and unusual punctuation in hostnames.
  • After commit, automated systems will pick up the new name in logs and monitoring tools.
Key Takeaway

Set a clear hostname, commit, and verify with show system hostname to confirm the active configuration reflects your change.

screens.title: Set a strong root password
screens.subtitle: Why the root account matters and how to secure it

narration.text: The root user on Junos has complete administrative privileges. That makes securing the root account one of the highest priority initial tasks. In configuration mode, you use set system root-authentication plain-text-password and the device will prompt you to enter and confirm the password. Choose a strong passphrase that mixes uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and symbols to resist guessing and brute-force attacks. A concrete example is creating a password that is at least twelve characters long and not reused from other systems. A common misconception is that creating a non-root admin removes the need to secure root — it does not; root remains a recovery account and will exist unless explicitly disabled, so its password must be strong. Best practice is to also create an unprivileged or limited admin for daily tasks and reserve root for recovery. Always commit after setting the password and verify you can authenticate as expected. Reflect: what policies would you enforce for root password rotation in your environment? Set a strong root password means set and commit a complex root password immediately; create non-root admin accounts for routine work to reduce root usage.. In practical terms, why the root account matters and how to secure it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Root security
keyIdea.text: Set and commit a complex root password immediately; create non-root admin accounts for routine work to reduce root usage.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Root Password
Secure step
# Set root password (device will prompt for the password)
user@router# set system root-authentication plain-text-password
# commit to apply
user@router# commit
The plain-text-password flow prompts you to type and confirm a password; the CLI avoids echoing the value. After commit, authenticate to verify.
Practical advice
  • Avoid using root for daily tasks; create a role-based admin account instead.
  • Pick a password manager to store complex passwords securely.
  • Plan periodic rotation and enforce strong password policies across devices.
Common mistake

Leaving the root password blank or using weak passwords exposes full device control to attackers.

screens.title: Configure NTP for accurate time
screens.subtitle: Why synchronized clocks matter for logs and certificates

narration.text: Network Time Protocol, or NTP, provides a reliable time source so the device clock matches other systems. Accurate time is essential for trustworthy logs, trouble-ticket correlation, and certificate validation. Without synchronized time you may find logs misordered, difficulty correlating events between devices, or TLS certificates reported as invalid. To configure an NTP server in Junos, enter configure mode and use set system ntp server followed by a server hostname or IP address, for example 1. pool. ntp. org. Commit the change and verify NTP status with show system ntp or operational show commands. A concrete example is setting an NTP pool for a lab device to ensure its logs align with your monitoring server. A common misconception is that NTP is optional; in practice, having correct timestamps is critical for troubleshooting and security auditing. Key takeaway: set an NTP server early in the device lifecycle and verify synchronization before relying on logs for incident analysis. Configure NTP for accurate time means configure ntp early so logs and certificates use accurate timestamps; verify synchronization as part of initial verification.. In practical terms, why synchronized clocks matter for logs and certificates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NTP importance
keyIdea.text: Configure NTP early so logs and certificates use accurate timestamps; verify synchronization as part of initial verification.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › NTP Configuration
Command
# Configure an NTP server
user@router# configure
[edit]
user@router# set system ntp server 1.pool.ntp.org
user@router# commit
# Verify NTP status (operational)
user@router> show system ntp
Using an NTP pool ensures redundancy. Replace the sample pool with your internal NTP server when present for lower latency and controlled time sources.
Why it matters
  • Accurate logs: timestamps across devices match, aiding troubleshooting.
  • Security: certificates and authentication can rely on consistent time.
  • Auditing: event correlation and incident timelines are trustworthy.
Key Takeaway

Configure and verify NTP early so logs and certificates use accurate, synchronized timestamps across your network.

screens.title: Enable SSH and create a non-root admin
screens.subtitle: Secure remote access and least-privilege administration

narration.text: Enabling SSH is a single command but part of a larger best-practice: prefer non-root accounts for routine work. Enable the SSH daemon with set system services ssh and commit. Then create a non-root user and grant appropriate privileges so day-to-day tasks do not require the root account. A concrete example: set system login user admin class super-user authentication plain-text-password to create an administrative user, then commit. This allows you to disable or limit direct root access if your policy requires it. A typical misconception is that enabling SSH alone completes security — it does not. You should also restrict which users can log in and from which source IPs when possible. After enabling SSH and creating a non-root admin, test SSH authentication and verify you can perform expected tasks. Key takeaway: enable SSH, create a limited admin for daily tasks, and reserve root for recovery to reduce risk from credential compromise. Enable SSH and create a non-root admin means enable ssh, create non-root admin accounts, and restrict access to follow least-privilege principles; always commit and test.. In practical terms, secure remote access and least-privilege administration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SSH & users
keyIdea.text: Enable SSH, create non-root admin accounts, and restrict access to follow least-privilege principles; always commit and test.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › SSH & Users
Commands
# Enable SSH and create a non-root admin
user@router> configure
[edit]
user@router# set system services ssh
user@router# set system login user admin class super-user authentication plain-text-password
user@router# commit
Commit to apply the SSH and user changes, then test by SSHing from your management workstation as the new admin account.
Best practices
  • Create non-root admins for daily tasks and reserve root for emergency use.
  • Restrict SSH access by source IP where possible.
  • Use strong password or public-key authentication and rotate credentials regularly.
Key Takeaway

Enable SSH and create role-based users. Test logins and minimize direct root usage to improve security posture.

screens.title: Common mistakes during initial configuration
screens.subtitle: What goes wrong and how to avoid it

narration.text: New device setup often reveals recurring mistakes that are easy to avoid when you know them. First, forgetting to commit is the most common error; you stage changes in the candidate configuration and then forget to run commit, leaving the device unchanged. A concrete example: you set system host-name but leave configure without committing — the running prompt still shows the old hostname. Second, incorrect command syntax or typos will lead to errors or unexpected settings. Use tab-completion and the question mark help to discover valid options. Third, leaving the root password blank or weak exposes full administrative control. Fourth, enabling SSH without proper user accounts or access restrictions creates a management plane you cannot safely control. To avoid these, always review changes with show | compare before commit, use tab-complete to ensure syntax, set a strong root password, create non-root admin accounts, and test each change immediately after commit. Reflect: which of these mistakes have you encountered and how did you detect them? Common mistakes during initial configuration means forgetting commit, syntax mistakes, weak root passwords, and untested ssh changes are common. review and test to avoid them.. In practical terms, what goes wrong and how to avoid it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoidable errors
keyIdea.text: Forgetting commit, syntax mistakes, weak root passwords, and untested SSH changes are common. Review and test to avoid them.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Common Mistakes

Mistake vs Fix

Forgetting commit — Fix: run show | compare, then commit, and verify with relevant show commands.
Syntax errors — Fix: use tab-completion and ? help to confirm command structure.
Weak root password — Fix: set a strong password and create non-root admins for daily work.
Unverified SSH changes — Fix: test SSH logins immediately after commit and restrict allowed sources.
Quick checklist
  • Review candidate with show | compare.
  • Commit when ready and test changes.
  • Keep a recovery plan — know how to rollback.
Common-mistake

Assuming a configured change is active without committing and verifying is how many outages start.

screens.title: Walkthrough: initial configuration exercise
screens.subtitle: A short sequence to perform on a new Junos device

narration.text: This hands-on walkthrough is the practical sequence you should complete on a new or virtual Junos device. Start at the console and log in. From operational mode run show version to confirm the device and show interfaces terse to identify the management interface. Enter configure and set the hostname to MyJNCIA-Router. Next set the root password using set system root-authentication plain-text-password and follow the prompts to enter a strong password. Configure NTP with set system ntp server 1. pool. ntp. org and enable SSH with set system services ssh. If you need a non-root admin, create one now with set system login user admin class super-user authentication plain-text-password. Before applying changes, run show | compare to inspect your candidate configuration. When satisfied, run commit to apply all changes. Exit configuration mode and verify the hostname with show system hostname and verify SSH by attempting an SSH connection from your workstation. A common mistake is skipping verification. After the exercise, ask: which verification step helped you detect a mistake and how? Walkthrough: initial configuration exercise means console → inspect → configure hostname/password/ntp/ssh → show | compare → commit → verify hostname and ssh connectivity.. In practical terms, a short sequence to perform on a new junos device. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Exercise flow
keyIdea.text: Console → inspect → configure hostname/password/NTP/SSH → show | compare → commit → verify hostname and SSH connectivity.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hands-on Walkthrough

Step-by-step

  1. Access the device via console and authenticate.
  2. Run show version and show interfaces terse to inspect the device.
  3. Enter configure and set hostname to MyJNCIA-Router.
  4. Set a strong root password and configure NTP and SSH.
  5. Run show | compare, then commit and verify with show system hostname and test SSH.
Starter code
# Console start
user@router> configure
[edit]
user@router# set system host-name MyJNCIA-Router
user@router# set system root-authentication plain-text-password
user@router# set system ntp server 1.pool.ntp.org
user@router# set system services ssh
user@router# commit
user@router# exit
user@router> show system hostname
Key Takeaway

Follow the sequence, review changes before committing, and verify active configuration to confirm success.

screens.title: Verifying changes and using show commands
screens.subtitle: How to confirm your changes are active and correct

narration.text: Verification closes the loop between configuring and operating a device. After a commit, you must confirm that the active configuration matches your intent. Standard verification commands include show system hostname to confirm the hostname, show interfaces terse to validate interface states and addresses, and show version to confirm software and platform. Use show | compare while in configuration mode to preview how the candidate differs from the active configuration. For connectivity tests, use ping and traceroute from operational mode to validate reachability. A concrete verification example: after committing NTP and SSH changes, run show system ntp and attempt an SSH login from a trusted workstation. A common misconception is that commit success equals success for all services; commit only guarantees the configuration is applied, not that runtime conditions are correct.
